lead: A limit state is a condition beyond which a structure, or one of its members, no longer does what it was designed to do. Limit state design, the method of IS 456:2000, checks every member against two families of limit states: collapse, which protects life, and serviceability, which protects use, appearance and durability. Each check uses its own loads and its own material values, chosen from statistics and partial safety factors. This chapter sets out the philosophy as the code states it, the limits it puts on deflection and cracking, and why it is preferred to the working stress and ultimate load methods.
prereq: You need: the working stress method and the ultimate load method.

blocks.text: The aim of design, in the words of most codes, is a structure that will, with an acceptable probability, stay fit for use during its life, sustain all the loads that are likely to occur, and resist misuse and fire well enough. Limit state design turns this into a set of checks: for each way a structure can stop doing its job, show that the chance of reaching that limit is small enough.

The chance is controlled in two steps. First, loads and strengths are described by characteristic values, statistical fractiles of their scatter (see characteristic strength and loads). Second, these are turned into design values by partial safety factors: loads are multiplied by γf, strengths divided by γm (see partial safety factors). The calculation itself is then deterministic; the probability sits behind the numbers.
The basic inequality for every limit state is
design action effect S<sub>d</sub> ≤ design resistance R<sub>d</sub>
blocks.where: S<sub>d</sub> is the moment, shear, axial force or torsion caused by the design loads; R<sub>d</sub> is the resistance of the section computed from design strengths. For a serviceability limit state the "resistance" is a limit such as span/250 or a crack width of 0.3 mm.

blocks.text: The limit states of collapse are reached when the member fails or becomes unstable. IS 456 lists:

items: Flexure: the section fails in bending. The stress block gives its resistance; tension steel should yield before the concrete crushes, so the failure gives warning.
Compression: a column crushes, alone or combined with bending; slender columns add buckling moments.
Shear: diagonal tension cracks; this is brittle, so stirrups are provided.
Torsion: twisting, combined with shear and bending, in edge beams and curved beams.

blocks.text: Other collapse limit states, such as loss of equilibrium (overturning or sliding of the whole structure) and failure under fire, are checked under the relevant rules. For collapse the loads are factored, usually γ<sub>f</sub> = 1.5 for dead plus live load, and the strengths are design strengths with γ<sub>m</sub> = 1.5 for concrete and 1.15 for steel.

Serviceability limit states are checked at service loads (γ<sub>f</sub> = 1.0, and 0.8 on live and wind load when both act with dead load) and with γ<sub>m</sub> = 1.0. IS 456 gives these limits for beams and slabs:

items: Deflection: the final deflection, including creep and shrinkage, measured from the level of the supports, must not exceed span/250. The deflection after the partitions and finishes are built must not exceed span/350 or 20 mm, whichever is less.

Cracking: the surface crack width should not exceed 0.3 mm in general. Where cracking is harmful because the member is always exposed to moisture or is in contact with soil or ground water, 0.2 mm is suggested; in a particularly aggressive environment, such as the severe exposure class, the limit is 0.004 times the nominal cover.
Others: vibration, durability (cover, grade and water–cement ratio for the exposure) and fire resistance.

blocks.text: In everyday design deflection is controlled by limiting the span to effective depth ratio (basic value 20 for simply supported beams, 7 for cantilevers and 26 for continuous beams, modified for steel stress and compression steel), and cracking by rules for bar spacing and cover. Those rules come with the design of beams and slabs.

sections.h3: Advantages of limit state design over other methods

blocks.text: In short: limit state design checks both safety and use; it puts safety where the uncertainty is, through separate factors; it uses the real inelastic strength of the materials; and it rests on measured scatter rather than judgement alone. Its cost is more checks and closer reliance on the code.

examples.question: A simply supported beam of span 6.0 m supports a floor with brick partitions. By calculation, its final total deflection is 22 mm and the part of the deflection that occurs after the partitions are built is 19 mm. Check both deflection limits of IS 456 and state what you would change.
steps: Final deflection limit = L/250 = 6000/250 = 24 mm. Actual 22 mm ≤ 24 mm: passes.
Limit after partitions = smaller of L/350 = 6000/350 = 17.1 mm and 20 mm, that is 17.1 mm.
Actual 19 mm > 17.1 mm: this limit fails, by 1.9 mm.

The beam is safe against collapse and passes the overall deflection check, yet it can crack the partitions. Increase the depth (deflection falls roughly with the cube of depth for the same load), or delay the building of the partitions so that more of the creep deflection happens before them.
examples.answer: Final deflection 22 mm ≤ 24 mm passes; deflection after partitions 19 mm > 17.1 mm fails, so the beam must be stiffened even though it is strong enough.

examples.question: Compare the moment a beam 230 mm wide with an effective depth of 450 mm (M20, Fe415) may carry at service load by the working stress method and by the limit state method, designed as a balanced singly reinforced section in each method. For the limit state method take M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 f<sub>ck</sub> b d² and γ<sub>f</sub> = 1.5.
steps: WSM: Q = 0.913 N/mm² (see working stress method). MR = Q b d² = 0.913 × 230 × 450² = 42.5 kNm, at service load.
LSM: M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 × 20 × 230 × 450² = 128.5 kNm, at factored load.
Service moment allowed by LSM = 128.5/1.5 = 85.7 kNm.

Ratio 85.7/42.5 = 2.0: the same concrete section carries about twice the service moment by limit state design, because it uses the material strength beyond the elastic range. It needs more steel to do so, and its deflection and cracking must then be checked.
examples.answer: WSM allows 42.5 kNm at service; LSM allows 128.5/1.5 = 85.7 kNm, about twice as much, subject to the serviceability checks.

traps: Serviceability is checked at service loads (γ<sub>f</sub> = 1.0) with γ<sub>m</sub> = 1.0, not at factored loads. Using 1.5 times the load in a deflection check overstates it by half.
Span/250 is the limit on the final deflection; the stricter limit after partitions is span/350 or 20 mm, whichever is less. For a 6 m span that is 17.1 mm, not 20 mm.
A section that passes the flexure check can still fail in shear: shear is a separate, brittle collapse limit state.
Limit state design is not "ultimate load method with a different factor": it adds serviceability checks and separate factors for each load and each material.
The probabilistic basis is in the choice of characteristic values and factors; the design calculation itself does not compute a probability.

quiz.a: A condition beyond which a structure or member no longer satisfies a design requirement, either of safety or of use.

quiz.q: Name the four limit states of collapse listed in IS 456 for members.
Why does limit state design check serviceability as well as collapse?
quiz.a: Collapse checks protect life; a safe member can still deflect, crack or vibrate so much that it cannot be used or its steel corrodes. Serviceability checks protect use, appearance and durability.

quiz.q: Give two advantages of the limit state method over the working stress method.
quiz.a: It checks collapse directly, using the inelastic strength of the materials, so sections are more economical; and it uses separate partial safety factors, so safety is placed where the uncertainty is.

quiz.q: Find both IS 456 deflection limits for a beam of span 7.5 m.
quiz.a: Final: 7500/250 = 30 mm. After partitions: smaller of 7500/350 = 21.4 mm and 20 mm, so 20 mm.

quiz.q: A slab of span 4.0 m deflects 18 mm in total. Does it pass the final deflection limit?
quiz.a: Limit = 4000/250 = 16 mm; 18 mm > 16 mm, so it fails.

quiz.q: The nominal cover of a beam in an aggressive environment is 50 mm. What is the limiting crack width, and why is it tied to the cover?
quiz.a: 0.004 × 50 = 0.2 mm. A crack is widest at the surface and narrows towards the bar; with more cover the bar sits deeper, so the code relates the allowed surface width to the cover.

quiz.q: Why can a section that satisfies S<sub>d</sub> ≤ R<sub>d</sub> in flexure still be unsafe?
quiz.a: Flexure is only one limit state. The same section must also satisfy the checks for shear and torsion (brittle modes), and the serviceability checks; passing one says nothing about the others.

beyond: Codes worldwide now calibrate their partial factors so that each limit state reaches a target reliability index over the design life; Eurocode 0 states this openly. Newer work adds limit states for fatigue, fire and earthquake performance, and performance-based design asks how much damage is acceptable at each level of hazard. Search next for "reliability index β", "performance-based seismic design" and "Eurocode 0 basis of design".

figure.caption: IS 456 asks two questions of every member: will it stand (collapse, at factored loads) and will it serve (deflection and cracking, at service loads). The bars are the 6 m beam of the first worked example: its final deflection passes, but the deflection after the partitions are built fails.
